atrophy

/AT-ruh-fee/ - the stress falls on AT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Atrophy means to waste away or weaken from lack of use.

Critics wrote that the director's imagination had atrophied across a decade of sequels, each film a fainter tracing of the first.

Example

Two seasons behind a desk, and the ranger who once built a fire in falling snow fumbled with damp matches for half an hour. Nothing injured her hands and nobody retrained them wrong; the skill had simply atrophied — unused, it thinned out like an unworked muscle, quietly, month by month.

Atrophy is the exact word because it names wasting away from disuse. She didn't forget in an instant and she wasn't taught badly; a capacity withered because nothing exercised it. That built-in cause — idleness, not attack — is what atrophy adds that 'weaken' alone doesn't.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

wither: To wither is to dry up and shrivel under outside punishment — drought, frost, scorching heat — and, figuratively, to shrink under hostile pressure. Atrophy needs no attacker at all: the wasting comes from disuse alone — nothing attacks the thing; it simply goes unexercised.

flag: To flag is to droop or lose vigor for a stretch — a runner's pace flags in the last mile, attention flags after lunch — a dip that passes when rest comes. Atrophy is slower and deeper: capacity wasting away over months of disuse, not sagging for an afternoon.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

strengthen: to build up force or capacity

flourish: to grow richly and thrive

Where it sits · how little is left to revive

weaken → atrophy → shrivel

weaken vs. atrophy: Anything can weaken a little and recover by Friday; atrophy is heavier — a steady wasting that sets in when something goes unused.

shrivel vs. atrophy: Shrivel goes further than atrophy: an atrophied skill has thinned and faded, but a shriveled one has dried to a husk with almost nothing left to revive.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — a-: without

Root — trophy: nourishment

Put it together: A- (without) + trophy (nourishment, from Greek trophe) = without feeding. To the Greeks, atrophia was the wasting of a body that isn't nourished; English kept the picture and widened it — muscles, skills, even institutions atrophy when nothing feeds or exercises them. The gym-shelf trophy is an unrelated look-alike, from a different Greek word for a victory monument.

Use the root in a new word: dystrophy: The school's charity run raised money for research into muscular dystrophy.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, with a clinical edge

Atrophy carries its cause inside it: things atrophy from disuse and idleness. If a thing is getting worse while being used — a road, a friendship under strain — the wider word is deteriorate, this unit's all-purpose decliner. Save atrophy for the muscle nobody flexes and the skill nobody practices.
